bpLabel: Fieldstrip Best Practices — this guide follows the single-action revolver care documented in A. Uberti’s own single-actions manual, and it takes nothing apart: the cylinder stays in the frame. It is not Traditions’s manual for this model. If you obtain the factory manual, follow it over this guide. Never take this firearm further apart than this guide goes.
cleanIntro:
No manual from Traditions exists for this model, but the revolver’s kind is documented: A. Uberti’s own single-actions book covers exactly this fixed-cylinder, loading-gate design, and this guide follows its care. Nothing comes apart — the cylinder stays in the frame, and every chamber is reached through the gate. If yours has no gate and the cylinder swings out to the side instead, this is the wrong guide.

Listed in Fieldstrip as .45 Colt. The chambering marked on the gun itself is the one that counts — not this guide, and not the listing.

steps.title: Ammunition out of the room, muzzle somewhere safe
steps.action: Before you start, put every loose cartridge, loaded magazine and box of ammunition in another room — a cleaning bench with live rounds on it is where unintended discharges happen. Keep the muzzle pointed where a shot would hurt no one, and keep your finger outside the trigger guard the whole time. Wear eye protection whenever you use solvent or work near a spring, and work where the air moves.
steps.prose: A safety, if yours has one, is never a substitute for an empty chamber, and nothing in this guide relies on one.

steps.title: A fixed cylinder means one chamber at a time
steps.action: This revolver’s cylinder does not swing out; it turns in the frame around its base pin, and you reach one chamber at a time through the loading gate on the right. That changes nothing about the standard — it only means the count matters: six chambers, checked one by one.
steps.quote: Unlike modern revolvers, which provide for the entire cylinder to rotate away from the frame exposing all bores or chambers, this single action revolver has a fixed cylinder which rotates around the cylinder base pin.
steps.cite: SINGLE ACTIONS, MODEL 'P', THUNDERER, LIGHTNING, MODEL 'P' JR., NEW SHERIFF, 1875, 1890 & BISLEY — ABSENT — no revision or edition line is printed — General Operation and Nomenclature, printed p.4
steps.warn: ALWAYS KEEP AN EMPTY CHAMBER BELOW THE HAMMER DURING TRANSPORTATION OR STORAGE.

steps.title: Gate open, hammer to the loading notch, every chamber punched clear
steps.action: Open the loading gate and draw the hammer back to its half-cock loading notch — the light click partway back that frees the cylinder to turn. Rotate each chamber in line with the gate and run the ejector rod its full stroke in each one. Then rotate the cylinder a full revolution, looking into every chamber as it passes the gate and touching each with a fingertip, and do that count a second time.
steps.quote: You must operate the ejector rod its full length in each chamber to ensure complete cartridge ejection.
steps.cite: SINGLE ACTIONS, MODEL 'P', THUNDERER, LIGHTNING, MODEL 'P' JR., NEW SHERIFF, 1875, 1890 & BISLEY — ABSENT — no revision or edition line is printed — Unloading, printed p.11
steps.warn: Move the hammer rearward to the half cock (loading) position and open the loading gate fully.

steps.title: No strip — the cylinder stays in
steps.action: The base pin stays in the frame, the cylinder stays on it, and the lockwork stays behind its screws. Every surface this clean needs is reachable through the gate and from the muzzle; anything deeper is Traditions’s work. The book’s own first demand before any cleaning begins is the one that matters.
steps.quote: Before beginning any cleaning or maintenance procedures, MAKE SURE the revolver is unloaded.
steps.cite: SINGLE ACTIONS, MODEL 'P', THUNDERER, LIGHTNING, MODEL 'P' JR., NEW SHERIFF, 1875, 1890 & BISLEY — ABSENT — no revision or edition line is printed — Cleaning and Maintenance, printed p.11
steps.warn: Failure to follow this step could lead to SERIOUS INJURY OR DEATH.

steps.title: No steel rod, and never reverse in the bore
steps.action: Use a wood, aluminium or brass rod — never steel — with a brass brush and correctly sized patches. Bore from the muzzle, each chamber through the gate, brushing all the way through before the stroke comes back.
steps.quote: To clean your revolver, use a wood, aluminum or brass cleaning rod (do not use steel), a brass bristle brush, and patches that are correctly sized to the caliber of your revolver.
steps.cite: SINGLE ACTIONS, MODEL 'P', THUNDERER, LIGHTNING, MODEL 'P' JR., NEW SHERIFF, 1875, 1890 & BISLEY — ABSENT — no revision or edition line is printed — Cleaning, printed p.11

steps.title: All the way through, every stroke
steps.action: Brush each bore and chamber full length, out the far end, then back — a brush reversed inside the bore sheds bristles and scores nothing clean. Then patches until one comes out clean, and the cylinder face and the barrel’s rear face brushed free of their blast ring.
steps.quote: Always brush all the way through the bore; never try to reverse directions while the brush is actually in the barrel or chamber.
steps.cite: SINGLE ACTIONS, MODEL 'P', THUNDERER, LIGHTNING, MODEL 'P' JR., NEW SHERIFF, 1875, 1890 & BISLEY — ABSENT — no revision or edition line is printed — Cleaning, printed p.11

steps.title: Oil the whole revolver, lightly
steps.action: A light film over the metal, a lightly oiled patch through the bore and each chamber for storage, and a dry patch through before it is next fired. Nothing runs into the lockwork.
steps.quote: Thereafter, completely, but lightly, oil the entire revolver.
steps.cite: SINGLE ACTIONS, MODEL 'P', THUNDERER, LIGHTNING, MODEL 'P' JR., NEW SHERIFF, 1875, 1890 & BISLEY — ABSENT — no revision or edition line is printed — Cleaning, printed p.11

steps.title: Look for the things that mean stop
steps.action: Hold the barrel up to the light and look through it: you want a clean, unbroken bore with no obstruction, no bulge and no dark ring. Look over the barrel, the cylinder and the frame for cracks, a bent ejector rod or a loose base pin catch, and for anything loose or missing. A screw or pin that has worked loose is reported, not tightened — how tight it should be is a question for Traditions.
steps.prose: Any one of these means the gun is not fired until Traditions has seen it.

deepAbsentReason: There is no deep clean for the Traditions 1873 Frontier, and this guide will not invent one. No manual from Traditions exists for this model; the pattern source documents a field strip and nothing deeper for an owner. Anything that needs more than this guide goes to Traditions, not onto the bench.

cleaning.name: BORE & CHAMBERS
tasks: Wood, aluminium or brass rod — never steel
All the way through, never reversed inside
A lightly oiled patch for storage; a dry patch before the next shot

cleaning.name: CYLINDER & FRAME
tasks: Cylinder face and the barrel’s rear face de-ringed
A light film of oil over the metal
⛔ No oil into the lockwork, and the base pin stays put

cleaning.name: EXTERIOR
tasks: Wiped with a lightly oiled cloth
No solvent on wood, finishes or optics

cleaning.name: STORAGE
tasks: Stored dry — never shut in a closed case while damp
Looked over for rust at every clean

reassembly.title: Gate closed, hammer down on an empty chamber
reassembly.action: Nothing came apart, so nothing goes back: close the loading gate, lower the hammer fully, and set the revolver down the way the book stores it — with an empty chamber under the hammer.
reassembly.quote: ALWAYS KEEP AN EMPTY CHAMBER BELOW THE HAMMER DURING TRANSPORTATION OR STORAGE.
reassembly.section: General Operation and Nomenclature, printed p.4

fncheck: Every chamber proven empty twice. Bring the hammer to its half-cock loading notch, open the gate, and turn the cylinder a full revolution: it must turn freely and click past each chamber in turn. Close the gate. This check never takes the hammer to full cock and never touches the trigger; a cylinder that binds or skips goes to Traditions.
